questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 4 month history of an aching lump on the right side of her lower abdomen. On standing there is a 3 cm soft, reducible swelling at the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis, below the level of the umbilicus. It has a cough impulse. She has never had abdominal surgery and her groins are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A Spigelian hernia passes through the linea semilunaris at the lateral border of rectus abdominis. Incisional hernias need a scar; epigastric and umbilical hernias are midline.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis
below the level of the umbilicus
steps.x: A reducible lump with a cough impulse at the **lateral edge of rectus**: the **linea semilunaris**.

elim: A midline ridge between the two rectus muscles, not a lateral lump.
Lies in the midline above the umbilicus.
Occurs at a previous surgical scar; she has had no surgery.
Lies at the umbilicus in the midline.

steps.x: **D. Spigelian hernia.** A hernia through the linea semilunaris is a Spigelian hernia.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man had an emergency midline laparotomy for a perforated ulcer 14 months ago, complicated by a wound infection. He smokes and has a BMI of 34. He now has a bulge in the middle of his abdomen that appears when he stands or coughs. There is a 6 cm soft, reducible swelling beneath the scar.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Incisional hernias occur at the site of previous surgery; wound infection, obesity and smoking increase the risk. Previous surgery is a general risk factor for hernias.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: appears when he stands or coughs
steps.x: A reducible swelling **under a laparotomy scar**, with wound infection, smoking and obesity as risks.

elim: A midline ridge on straining without a defect or previous scar.
A small midline defect in the linea alba above the umbilicus, not at a scar.
Soft but has no cough impulse and does not reduce.
Lies at the lateral edge of rectus, not in a midline scar.

steps.x: **C. Incisional hernia.** A hernia at the site of previous surgery is an incisional hernia.

questions.stem: A 5 month old girl is brought by her father because her belly button bulges when she cries. She is feeding well and thriving. On examination there is a 1.5 cm soft swelling at the umbilicus that reduces easily with gentle pressure and is not tender. Her groins are normal. She was born at 34 weeks.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Umbilical hernias are common in infants, obesity and pregnancy, and carry a low risk of incarceration. Small ones in babies usually resolve by 12 months.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: soft swelling at the umbilicus that reduces easily
steps.x: A soft, **reducible** swelling **at the umbilicus** that appears on crying in a **preterm infant**.

elim: Lies above the umbilicus in the linea alba.
Bowel covered by a membrane outside the abdomen at birth, not a reducible skin-covered bulge.
Uncovered bowel beside the umbilicus at birth.
A moist red nodule in the stump, not a reducible bulge.

steps.x: **E. Umbilical hernia.** Umbilical hernias are common in infants (especially preterm) and have a low incarceration risk.

questions.stem: A baby boy develops respiratory distress minutes after birth at term. His respiratory rate is 80 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air. His abdomen looks flat and sunken. Breath sounds are reduced on the left and bowel sounds are heard over the left chest. The heart sounds are loudest on the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bowel sounds in the chest of a neonate in respiratory distress mean a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Abdominal contents in the chest leave the abdomen scaphoid and push the heart across.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: bowel sounds are heard over the left chest
heart sounds are loudest on the right
steps.x: A neonate in **respiratory distress** with **bowel sounds in the chest**, a scaphoid abdomen and mediastinal shift.

elim: Follows meconium-stained liquor; it does not put bowel sounds in the chest.
Surfactant deficiency in preterm babies; the abdomen is normal.
Shifts the heart away but gives a hyper-resonant chest with no bowel sounds.
Mild, self-limiting, often after caesarean section; no bowel sounds in the chest.

steps.x: **A. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia.** Bowel sounds on respiratory examination of a neonate in respiratory distress = diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man is brought in after a fall from a ladder. He was talking at the scene but is now drowsy. His GCS has fallen from 14 to 8 over 30 minutes. His pulse rate is 52 bpm and BP 182/96 mmHg. His right pupil is fixed and dilated; the left reacts normally. CT shows a large right-sided extradural haematoma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his pupil finding?
questions.e: Uncal herniation squeezes the medial temporal lobe over the tentorium and compresses CN III, giving an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil. It is a neurosurgical emergency.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of his pupil finding? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: right pupil is fixed and dilated
steps.x: A falling GCS with a **unilateral fixed dilated pupil** on the side of the haematoma.

elim: Compresses the medulla, causing respiratory arrest rather than a unilateral fixed pupil.
Causes a small pupil with ptosis, not a fixed dilated pupil.
Causes painful visual loss with a relative afferent defect, not a fixed dilated pupil.
Shifts the cingulate gyrus under the falx; it does not compress the third nerve.

steps.x: **E. Uncal herniation.** Uncal herniation compresses the oculomotor nerve (CN III): ipsilateral dilated pupil.

questions.stem: An 83 year old woman has a 2 day history of a painful lump in her right groin. It lies below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle, and is irreducible, tender and red. She is eating, has not vomited, is passing flatus and opened her bowels this morning. Her abdomen is soft and not distended. Her temperature is 37.9°C.
questions.q: Which type of hernia is most likely?
questions.e: In a Richter's hernia only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so it can strangulate without causing obstruction. Femoral hernias in older women carry a high strangulation risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which type of hernia is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: passing flatus and opened her bowels this morning
steps.x: A **strangulated-looking** femoral hernia but **no obstruction**: bowels open, no vomiting, no distension.

elim: Contains a Meckel's diverticulum; it is not defined by the absence of obstruction.
Part of the sac wall is formed by a viscus such as the colon or bladder.
Lies at the lateral edge of rectus, not below the inguinal ligament.
Lies at the umbilicus.

steps.x: **B. Richter's hernia.** Strangulation without obstruction symptoms = Richter's hernia (only part of the bowel wall is trapped).

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has a known right inguinal hernia that has always gone back when he lies down. For 2 days he has been unable to push it back. It is mildly uncomfortable. The swelling is firm, mildly tender and slightly pink, with a cough impulse. He is not vomiting and is passing flatus. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An incarcerated hernia is irreducible, may be erythematous and tender, and keeps its cough impulse. It is at high risk of progressing to strangulation, so he needs urgent surgical review.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: mildly tender and slightly pink, with a cough impulse
steps.x: **Irreducible** but only mildly tender, keeps its **cough impulse**, with no systemic upset or obstruction.

elim: Lies in the scrotum, transilluminates and has no cough impulse.
Nodes do not have a cough impulse and are not a previously reducible lump.
He cannot reduce it.
Would be very painful, hot, discoloured and tender with systemic upset and often obstruction.

steps.x: **B. Incarcerated inguinal hernia.** Incarcerated = irreducible, may be red/tender, retains cough impulse; high risk of strangulation.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had a left groin lump for years. Over the past month he has had brief episodes of pain in it that settled on their own. For 8 hours the pain has been constant and he has vomited four times. The lump is irreducible, dusky purple and hot. His abdomen is distended with high-pitched bowel sounds. His pulse rate is 112 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Strangulation causes recent colour change, irreducibility, tenderness and heat, often after episodes of pain that settled. Bowel sounds suggesting obstruction confirm bowel is trapped.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: brief episodes of pain in it that settled
steps.x: Preceding **intermittent pain**, then an **irreducible, discoloured, hot** lump with **obstruction**.

elim: A tender epididymis and testis, often with urinary symptoms; it does not cause bowel obstruction.
A hot tender swelling, but not a long-standing lump with bowel obstruction.
Irreducible but without colour change, heat and systemic upset.
Sudden testicular pain in a young male; the testis is high-riding, not a groin lump.

steps.x: **D. Strangulated inguinal hernia.** Strangulation: recent colour change, irreducible, tender, warm, with obstruction.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy is brought by his mother because a lump appears in his right groin when he coughs or cries. It disappears when he lies down. He is otherwise well. On examination while he is crying there is a soft bulge just lateral to the right pubic tubercle. His testes are both in the scrotum.
questions.q: Which type of hernia is most likely?
questions.e: Inguinal hernias in children are always indirect, through a patent processus vaginalis. They are commoner in boys and on the right, and bulge lateral to the pubic tubercle on crying.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which type of hernia is most likely? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: lateral to the right pubic tubercle
steps.x: A **boy**, **right-sided**, bulging on crying **lateral to the pubic tubercle**.

elim: Is an acquired weakness of older adults; children's inguinal hernias are indirect.
Very rare in children and lies below the inguinal ligament.
Occurs at the lateral edge of rectus, not in the groin.
Lies at the umbilicus.

steps.x: **C. Indirect inguinal hernia.** Inguinal hernias in children are always indirect (patent processus vaginalis), commoner in boys and on the right.

questions.stem: An 87 year old woman with a BMI of 17 has 3 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. She has no previous surgery and her groins and umbilicus are normal. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm. Rectal examination reveals a tender mass on the right side of the pelvis. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her obstruction?
questions.e: An obturator hernia gives a tender mass on rectal examination, classically in thin elderly women with small bowel obstruction and no external hernia or previous surgery.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely cause of her obstruction? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no previous surgery and her groins and umbilicus are normal
tender mass on the right side of the pelvis
steps.x: A **thin, elderly woman** with small bowel obstruction, **no scar or external hernia**, and a **tender mass per rectum**.

elim: The commonest cause of small bowel obstruction, but she has had no surgery.
Would give a lump below the inguinal ligament; her groins are normal.
Causes large bowel symptoms and a hard rectal mass, not small bowel obstruction with a tender pelvic mass.
Gives massive large bowel distension, not small bowel loops.

steps.x: **C. Obturator hernia.** Obturator hernia: tender mass per rectum in a thin elderly woman with obstruction.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has a 3 month history of a lump in her left groin that is uncomfortable after long shifts as a nurse. On standing there is a 3 cm soft, reducible swelling with a cough impulse. Its neck lies above the inguinal ligament, superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. There is no lump in the thigh.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A hernia superior and medial to the pubic tubercle is inguinal. Inguinal hernias are the commonest type overall, even in women; femoral hernias lie inferolateral to it.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: superior and medial to the pubic tubercle
steps.x: The key is the **position relative to the pubic tubercle**: superior and medial.

elim: Lies below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
Firm nodes without a cough impulse that do not reduce.
A fluctuant lump with fever and back pain.
Lies below the ligament at the saphenofemoral junction and has a thrill on coughing.

steps.x: **B. Inguinal hernia.** Superior and medial to the pubic tubercle = inguinal; inferolateral = femoral. Inguinal is the commonest hernia even in women.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man who works as a builder has a 2 month history of a dragging feeling in his right groin that is worse after lifting. On standing there is a soft swelling superior and medial to the pubic tubercle that gets bigger when he coughs. He can push it back when lying down. The examiner can feel above the swelling and both testes are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An inguinal hernia is a reducible groin lump with a cough impulse that enlarges on standing or straining. A scrotal lump you cannot get above would suggest inguinoscrotal extension.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: dragging feeling in his right groin
push it back when lying down
steps.x: A groin lump with a **dragging** sensation, **cough impulse**, **reducible**, in a man who **lifts**.

elim: Is in the scrotum, transilluminates and has no cough impulse.
Is soft but irreducible and has no cough impulse.
Lies below the inguinal ligament and disappears on lying, with a thrill on coughing.
A 'bag of worms' in the scrotum that is above the testis, not a groin lump.

steps.x: **B. Inguinal hernia.** Groin lump + cough impulse + reducible, superior and medial to the pubic tubercle = inguinal hernia.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has a reducible indirect inguinal hernia diagnosed in clinic. He has no pain and wants to know the risk of it becoming strangulated before deciding about surgery. The surgeon explains the risk and how it compares with other types of groin hernia.
questions.q: Which statement about his strangulation risk is most accurate?
o: No risk while the hernia is reducible
Up to 3% each year, higher than for a femoral hernia
Up to 3% each year, more common in direct than indirect hernias
Up to 3% each year, more common in indirect than direct hernias
questions.e: The annual probability of strangulation of an inguinal hernia is up to 3%, more common in indirect hernias. Femoral hernias strangulate more often than inguinal ones.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which statement about his strangulation risk is most accurate? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **reducible indirect** inguinal hernia: recall the annual figure and which type strangulates more.

elim: Far too high.
Any hernia can become irreducible and strangulate.
Femoral hernias carry a higher strangulation risk than inguinal hernias.
Strangulation is commoner in indirect hernias.

steps.x: **E. Up to 3% each year, more common in indirect than direct hernias.** Inguinal hernia: annual strangulation probability up to 3%, commoner in indirect hernias; femoral is higher still.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man who plays football has a 3 month history of right groin pain when he sprints or kicks. He has noticed no lump. On examination standing and lying there is no palpable swelling and no cough impulse, though the right groin is slightly tender. His hips have a full range of movement.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Hernias are diagnosed clinically; when the diagnosis is uncertain, ultrasound is the next test. It is dynamic, quick and radiation-free.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: no palpable swelling and no cough impulse
right groin pain when he sprints
steps.x: Groin pain suggesting a hernia but **nothing to feel**: the diagnosis is **uncertain clinically**.

elim: Does not show a groin hernia.
Involves radiation and is not the first test for an uncertain groin hernia.
Too invasive as a diagnostic step.
His hips move fully; it would not show a hernia.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound of the groin.** Hernia diagnosis is clinical; if uncertain, ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has a 6 month history of a lump in his left groin. On standing there is a 4 cm soft swelling superior and medial to the left pubic tubercle. It has a clear cough impulse and reduces fully when he lies down. He is referred for surgical repair and asks what scan he needs to confirm it is a hernia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: The gold standard is clinical diagnosis by history and examination. Ultrasound is kept for when the diagnosis is uncertain.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: superior and medial to the left pubic tubercle
steps.x: A **classic reducible groin lump with a cough impulse**: there is no doubt about the diagnosis.

elim: Unnecessary radiation when the diagnosis is clinically clear.
An invasive contrast study, rarely used.
Not needed when examination is diagnostic.
Used only when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain.

steps.x: **A. Clinical examination alone.** The gold standard for hernia diagnosis is clinical history and examination; image only if uncertain.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has a reducible right groin hernia that extends towards the scrotum. With him lying down, the surgeon reduces the hernia fully and then presses firmly over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament before asking him to stand and cough.
questions.q: Which finding would confirm an indirect inguinal hernia?
o: Hernia appears below the inguinal ligament
Hernia does not reappear on coughing
Hernia reappears medial to the pressure point
questions.e: An indirect hernia passes through the deep inguinal ring, so pressure over the ring stops it reappearing on coughing. A direct hernia still bulges medially.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which finding would confirm an indirect inguinal hernia? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: presses firmly over the midpoint of the inguinal ligament
steps.x: Pressure over the **deep inguinal ring** (above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament) blocks the indirect hernia's route.

elim: Describes a saphena varix.
Suggests a femoral hernia.
Suggests a direct hernia through Hesselbach's triangle.
Suggests a hydrocele.

steps.x: **C. Hernia does not reappear on coughing.** Deep ring occlusion test: an indirect hernia is controlled and does not reappear on coughing.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has a 1.5 cm firm lump in her right groin noticed 3 weeks ago. It lies below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle. It is not tender, does not reduce and has no definite cough impulse. Her legs, feet and perineum have no wounds. The GP is unsure whether it is a hernia or a lymph node.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: When the diagnosis is uncertain, ultrasound is used. A lump inferolateral to the pubic tubercle may be a femoral hernia, which has a high strangulation risk.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle
unsure whether it is a hernia or a lymph node
steps.x: A lump in the **femoral hernia position** but the **clinical diagnosis is uncertain**.

elim: Will not show a small groin lump.
Risks puncturing bowel if this is a femoral hernia.
For staging known cancer, not a first test for a groin lump.
A possible femoral hernia needs urgent assessment because of strangulation risk.

steps.x: **D. Ultrasound of the groin.** Uncertain hernia diagnosis: ultrasound. A femoral hernia must not be missed.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man is found to have a small left inguinal hernia at a health check. It causes no pain and does not limit his activities. It reduces easily and has a cough impulse. He would prefer to avoid an operation if it is safe to do so. He has no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Small asymptomatic inguinal hernias can be managed by watchful waiting, with safety-netting about pain, irreducibility and vomiting that suggest strangulation or obstruction.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **small, asymptomatic, reducible** inguinal hernia in a man who wants to avoid surgery.

elim: There are no features of strangulation or obstruction.
Used for bilateral or recurrent hernias; he would prefer to avoid surgery.
For irreducible or strangulated hernias.
For high-risk or frail patients with symptoms.

steps.x: **E. Watchful waiting with safety-netting.** Small asymptomatic inguinal hernia: watchful waiting, safety-net for strangulation or obstruction.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has an aching right groin lump that limits his work as a delivery driver. On standing there is a broad, reducible swelling superior and medial to the right pubic tubercle with a cough impulse. Pressure over the deep inguinal ring does not control it. His left groin is normal. He has not had previous groin surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A symptomatic, uncomplicated, unilateral direct inguinal hernia is treated by elective open mesh repair, which has a low recurrence rate. Laparoscopic repair is for bilateral or recurrent hernias.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Pressure over the deep inguinal ring does not control it
steps.x: A **symptomatic, unilateral, uncomplicated** hernia not controlled at the deep ring: **direct**.

elim: For irreducible or strangulated hernias.
Preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernias.
For patients at high surgical risk or with low life expectancy.
He is symptomatic, so repair is indicated.

steps.x: **A. Elective open mesh repair.** Direct, uncomplicated, unilateral: elective open mesh repair (lower recurrence).

questions.stem: A 58 year old man had an open mesh repair of a right inguinal hernia 4 years ago. He now has a new reducible lump with a cough impulse at the same site, which aches when he lifts at work. His left groin is normal. He is fit and keen to have it fixed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Recurrent (and bilateral) inguinal hernias are best repaired laparoscopically with mesh, avoiding the scarred anterior approach.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: open mesh repair of a right inguinal hernia 4 years ago
steps.x: A **recurrent** inguinal hernia after a previous open repair.

elim: Reserved for irreducible or strangulated hernias.
Going back through scarred tissue raises the risk of complications; recurrent hernias are repaired laparoscopically.
For frail, high-risk patients.
He is symptomatic and wants repair.

steps.x: **B. Laparoscopic mesh repair.** Bilateral or recurrent inguinal hernias: laparoscopic mesh repair.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has a strangulated right inguinal hernia. He has had IV fluids and antibiotics and is taken to theatre as an emergency. At operation the hernia contains a loop of small bowel that is dark and non-viable, and there is contaminated fluid in the sac. The bowel is resected.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to repair the hernia defect?
o: Leave the defect and apply a truss
questions.e: Irreducible or strangulated hernias are repaired with an open non-mesh technique. Mesh is avoided in a contaminated field because of infection.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate way to repair the hernia defect? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
An **emergency** strangulated hernia with **non-viable bowel** and **contamination**.

elim: Planned surgery for bilateral or recurrent hernias, not an emergency with contamination.
A truss does not treat a strangulated hernia.
Mesh in a contaminated field risks infection; it is for uncomplicated hernias.
Not an option once strangulation has occurred.

steps.x: **D. Open non-mesh repair.** Irreducible or strangulated: open non-mesh repair.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man presents to the emergency department with 6 hours of a very painful, irreducible, red, tender left groin lump and two episodes of vomiting. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. A junior doctor suggests giving morphine and trying to push the hernia back under sedation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Urgent surgical review for emergency surgery
questions.e: A strangulated hernia needs urgent surgical review and emergency surgery. Manual reduction is not recommended because non-viable bowel may be returned to the abdomen.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Strangulated** hernia: irreducible, red, tender, systemically unwell and vomiting.

elim: This is an emergency.
A truss does not treat strangulation.
Not recommended for a strangulated hernia; it may push dead bowel back into the abdomen.
Delays treatment; the diagnosis is clinical.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical review for emergency surgery.** Complicated (irreducible or strangulated) hernia: urgent surgical review or emergency surgery; do not manually reduce.

questions.stem: A 9 month old boy is seen by the GP with 4 hours of inconsolable crying and two vomits. His mother noticed a lump in his right groin yesterday that has become hard and red. The lump is irreducible and he screams when it is touched. His pulse rate is 168 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Refer to paediatric surgery within 2 months
Try to reduce the hernia in the surgery
questions.e: A child with a strangulated hernia needs emergency herniotomy, so the GP calls 999 for urgent hospital assessment. Delayed review risks bowel and testicular infarction.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
An infant with an **irreducible, red, tender** groin lump and **vomiting**: a **strangulated hernia**.

elim: A strangulated hernia can cause bowel infarction within hours.
The timing for an uncomplicated hernia in an older child.
Delays emergency treatment.
Manual reduction of a strangulated hernia is not recommended.

steps.x: **A. Call 999 for urgent hospital assessment.** Child with strangulated hernia: call 999 for urgent hospital assessment and emergency herniotomy.

questions.stem: A 91 year old man with severe heart failure and an ejection fraction of 20% has a large right inguinal hernia that aches when he walks. It reduces easily and is not tender. He lives in a nursing home and the anaesthetist judges him at very high surgical risk. He would like help with the discomfort.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Open mesh repair under general anaesthesia
Truss with surgical referral if no improvement
questions.e: For patients at high surgical risk or with low life expectancy, a truss support belt can control symptoms, with surgical referral if there is no improvement.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A **symptomatic, reducible** hernia in a man at **very high surgical risk**.

elim: For irreducible or strangulated hernias.
Requires general anaesthesia; he is at very high surgical risk.
His surgical risk is too high for an elective operation now.
He is symptomatic and wants help with the discomfort.

steps.x: **D. Truss with surgical referral if no improvement.** High surgical risk or low life expectancy: a truss support belt, with surgical referral if no improvement.

questions.stem: A 4 week old baby boy is brought to the GP because his mother has noticed a swelling in his right groin when he cries. It disappears when he settles. He is feeding well and has no vomiting. On examination there is a soft, reducible swelling lateral to the right pubic tubercle and both testes are in the scrotum.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Refer to paediatric surgery for correction within 2 days
Refer to paediatric surgery for correction within 2 months
Refer to paediatric surgery for correction within 2 weeks
questions.e: Young infants have the highest risk of incarceration. A congenital inguinal hernia under 6 weeks of age should be corrected within 2 days by paediatric surgery.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: soft, reducible swelling lateral to the right pubic tubercle
steps.x: A **congenital inguinal hernia** in a baby **under 6 weeks old**.

elim: Inguinal hernias do not resolve; this applies to umbilical hernias.
The timing for a child aged 6 months to 6 years.
The timing for a baby aged 6 weeks to 6 months.
Not used for infants.

steps.x: **B. Refer to paediatric surgery for correction within 2 days.** Congenital inguinal hernia timing: under 6 weeks within 2 days; under 6 months within 2 weeks; under 6 years within 2 months.

questions.stem: A 3 year old girl has a soft lump in her left groin that appears when she runs and disappears when she lies down. It has never been painful or stuck out. She is well. On examination there is a small reducible swelling lateral to the left pubic tubercle. Her parents ask when it will be fixed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure that it will resolve by age 5
